name: Material participation
lead: An STR tax plan needs an operating record that matches the participation test being used. The number of hours is only one part of the analysis; the type of work, who else performs it, the rental activity and the tax year also matter.
sections: Build the record while the work happens

Record the date, property, task and actual time spent on operating work. Keep the supporting emails, invoices and calendar entries with the log. Ask the CPA which activities count before adding travel, education or investor research. A detailed record is more useful than a round number reconstructed at year end.
Match the test to the operating arrangement

The more-than-100-hour test also requires that no other individual participate more. A separate test concerns substantially all participation. Hiring a co-host does not automatically settle either test. Review the actual division of work and the activity classification with the tax adviser for each year.
Keep the investment decision separate

Do not manufacture work or change the records to fit a desired deduction. Ask for a written explanation of the test, the evidence and any limitations. An attractive tax illustration cannot replace a viable property budget and an operating plan you can actually carry out.
official: IRS Publication 925: participation and passive activity rules

name: Depreciation and tax planning
lead: A tax deduction and cash in the bank are different things. A useful STR plan explains which assets create the deduction, whether the owner can use the loss, when the property is ready for its intended use and how the plan affects later years.
sections: Separate the asset calculation from the tax result

An acquisition includes components with different tax treatment. Land is not depreciable, and the entire purchase price is not automatically eligible for bonus depreciation. Have the CPA reconcile the purchase allocation, improvement costs and any cost-segregation study before estimating a benefit.
Model cash flow before adding a tax illustration

Prepare the operating budget, debt schedule, setup costs and reserve first. Then show the tax effect as a separate scenario. A deduction multiplied by an assumed tax rate is an illustration, not a promised refund. The ability to use losses depends on the taxpayer's facts and applicable limitations.
Review timing and later-year consequences

Record acquisition and placed-in-service dates, rental use and supporting invoices. Ask the adviser to compare current federal rules, state treatment, future deductions and a later sale or change of use. A strategy that accelerates deductions changes timing; it does not make purchase costs or investment risk disappear.

name: Seller and creative financing
lead: Seller financing changes how a purchase is funded, but the property still has to support its costs and obligations. Compare the cash required today with the payment schedule, remaining principal, balloon date and the conditions for a future refinance.
sections: Write out the entire payment structure

Compare the purchase price, down payment, interest, amortization, balloon and all closing costs in one schedule. Include any underlying loan and servicing charge. Lower cash at closing can leave more reserves, but it does not by itself make the transaction cheaper or more profitable.
Give the documents the same attention as the economics

Have a qualified local attorney and the closing professionals review title, lien priority, existing loan restrictions, insurance and default remedies. A subject-to purchase and a new seller note are different structures. Do not assume the seller's agreement removes the rights of an existing lender.
Choose an exit that survives a difficult year

Test the debt against lower bookings and higher expenses. Model what happens if the property cannot be refinanced at the expected rate or valuation before the balloon is due. Keep payments documented through the agreed servicing process and resolve discrepancies before they become a closing or default problem.

name: Loans and cash to close
lead: The right loan is the one whose permitted use, total cost and payment risk fit the property. Comparing only a down-payment percentage or advertised rate misses costs that can change both launch liquidity and ongoing cash flow.
sections: Compare the same transaction on each quote

Ask lenders to price the same property, occupancy, borrower and closing date. Compare points, origination, other lender fees, prepaid items, escrow funding and cash to close. Confirm the rate-lock period and what changes if the appraisal or closing date moves.
Confirm the intended rental use

Tell the lender exactly how the property will be used. A second-home product, investment loan and DSCR product can have different eligibility and occupancy requirements. Low down-payment language in an older recording is not evidence that the same product is available or permitted for today's transaction.
Preserve the operating reserve

Include furnishings, repairs, permits and zero-revenue carrying time after closing. Test payments at the actual quoted rate and any reset or balloon terms. A lower initial cash requirement is helpful only when the remaining reserve can support the launch and a slower booking period.

name: Equity and refinancing
lead: Equity can support the next investment, but it is not spendable cash until a sale or a lender-approved refinance occurs. Separate an estimated property value from the amount that can actually be borrowed after costs, eligibility checks and debt limits.
sections: Calculate usable equity rather than headline value

Start with a supportable valuation, subtract the existing debt and apply the proposed lender's leverage limit. Then subtract refinancing costs, penalties and required reserves. A property can appreciate while producing little cash available for another purchase.
Test the new payment before taking cash out

A refinance may increase the balance, change the rate and extend repayment. Rebuild the operating budget using the proposed debt service, rather than assuming the earlier cash flow continues. Keep a case in which the refinance is delayed or unavailable.
Compare hold, refinance and sale deliberately

Review expected operating cash, transaction costs, tax consequences, ownership documents and the capital needed elsewhere. A video example describes a particular strategy, not a universal instruction to hold forever or borrow more. Bring the actual statements and ownership agreement to the relevant advisers.

name: Design and furnishing
lead: A rental improvement should serve a defined guest and fit a complete launch budget. Attractive photos can help a property compete, but the proposed work also has to be legal, insurable, maintainable and supported by evidence from comparable listings.
sections: Connect each improvement to the guest experience

Identify the group size, reason for travel and features guests actually value in this market. Compare similar homes with and without the proposed feature. Separate an observed difference in listings from a proven increase in booked revenue; neither a popular amenity nor a polished rendering guarantees a return.
Get comparable scopes before comparing prices

Ask competing teams to price the same rooms, furniture quantities, installation, freight, assembly, disposal and contractor work. Identify owner approvals, allowances and exclusions. A lower headline quote can become more expensive if important setup work is omitted.
Budget the operating life of the improvement

Include cleaning, servicing, replacement, insurance and any permit or safety review. Confirm the installation schedule, access and inspection responsibilities before promising a launch date. Prioritize the improvements that meet the guest need and remain affordable in the conservative operating case.

name: Co-hosting and operations
lead: A co-hosting arrangement works best when responsibilities, fees and reporting are explicit. Delegating daily work can reduce the owner's workload, but ownership still includes funding decisions, oversight and responsibility for the provider relationships.
sections: Define who owns each operating task

List guest communication, pricing, cleaning, maintenance, restocking and after-hours response. Set spending limits and escalation rules. Ask who hires local workers, who checks the completed work and who supplies backup coverage when the primary contact is unavailable.
Compare fees with the same revenue definition

Establish whether a percentage applies to accommodation revenue, cleaning fees or another amount. Review onboarding, software, maintenance markups and termination costs as well. A lower quoted percentage does not establish better net performance if the scope or fee base differs.
Keep access and reporting under control

Agree on owner access to calendars, listing accounts, payout records and performance reports. Review revenue, expenses, guest issues and upcoming repairs on a regular schedule. If the relationship changes, document account transfers, future bookings, deposits and vendor access before the old arrangement ends.

name: Rules and property permissions
lead: An STR strategy depends on permission for the actual address and intended use. A city's reputation, an existing listing or a seller's assurance does not establish that a new owner can operate the same rental after closing.
sections: Verify the property rather than the market label

Check the relevant zoning, rental permit, occupancy, parking and operating requirements with the responsible authority. Obtain the HOA or covenant documents when applicable. Ask whether existing permits transfer and what happens during a change in ownership or use.
Keep the ownership and operating documents consistent

Tell the lender, insurer, closing team and relevant advisers how the property will be owned and operated. An LLC does not by itself approve a rental use, settle coverage or eliminate personal guarantees. Lease-based arbitrage requires its own written permissions and cost review.
Put unresolved facts into the purchase decision

Record the source, date and exact address for each answer. Give unresolved approvals an owner and a deadline while contractual protections still apply. If a restriction changes the available nights or guest capacity, revise the economics before committing money to the purchase or setup.

name: Market selection
lead: A useful market comparison connects guest demand to the cost of a suitable property. A popular destination can still produce weak economics if purchase prices, restrictions, financing or operating expenses absorb the available revenue.
sections: Compare the same guest and property segment

Match the bedroom count, location, amenities, guest capacity and service standard. Review a full seasonal cycle rather than extrapolating from a holiday weekend. A large group home and a small apartment can face different competitors even within the same city.
Read supply and revenue together

Ask whether a change in listing counts reflects regulation, seasonality, data coverage or genuine competitive exits. Reconcile nightly rates with booked nights and owner blocks. Fewer listings do not automatically mean the remaining homes will receive more profitable bookings.
Take the market idea back to an address

Obtain property-specific insurance, tax, management and repair estimates, then test the financing and permit path. Build a conservative case using the same complete cost categories in each market. Use dated market discussion as a research starting point and verify the conditions again before making an offer.

name: Client stories and examples
lead: A client story helps explain an investment process, but one property's experience cannot establish the result another buyer will receive. Read the period, cash invested and expense definitions alongside every revenue or tax number.
sections: Identify what each number measures

Distinguish gross booking revenue, net operating income, cash after debt and a tax illustration. Ask whether the period is a full year, a strong month or a forward projection. Keep the actual purchase and setup costs alongside the results so the denominator is visible.
Understand the work behind the example

Look at sourcing, financing, diligence, design, launch and operating handoff separately. Identify which decisions were made by the owner and which providers performed the work. An impressive outcome does not show that the same property, terms or operating team will be available again.
Use the story to prepare better questions

Request the underlying records that would let you reconcile the headline to a property budget. Ask what went differently from the plan and how slower months were funded. Apply the lessons to your own capital, timeline and risk tolerance before drawing a conclusion about a purchase.

name: Cash flow and underwriting
lead: An STR investment has to work as an operating business. The useful question is how much cash remains after the full cost of owning, funding and running the property, including the money required to launch and maintain it.
sections: Reconcile revenue to a supportable operating case

Compare similar listings and review seasonality, available nights, rates and owner blocks. Separate actual payout records from projections. A high gross yield or occupancy rate can still conceal weak cash flow when the underlying costs or pricing assumptions are incomplete.
Include the costs that arrive outside the headline

Model property taxes, insurance, utilities, management, repairs, replacement reserves, booking costs and debt service. Add purchase costs, furnishings, improvements and startup carrying time to the cash invested. Avoid mixing a percentage of purchase price with a percentage of revenue.
Stress the decision before making an offer

Test lower revenue, a slower launch, unexpected repairs and the actual financing terms. Keep the tax scenario separate from operating cash so the investment remains understandable without assuming a refund. Set an offer ceiling from the conservative case and revisit it when new evidence changes the budget.

name: Acquisition process
lead: A successful purchase starts with a clear plan for capital, timing and the work between the first call and an operating rental. Each handoff needs an owner, a deliverable and a decision deadline.
sections: Define the purchase before looking for a shortcut

Write down your available capital, reserve, financing path, preferred operating model and the risks you will not accept. These criteria make it easier to screen a property consistently and avoid being pulled toward a headline result that does not fit your circumstances.
Turn the process into specific responsibilities

Map sourcing, underwriting, negotiation, inspection, financing, closing, design and management. Ask the acquisition team which tasks are included, which are introductions to independent providers and which decisions remain yours. Use the written agreement to resolve overlaps and exclusions.
Finish with an operating handoff

Before closing, confirm the setup budget, provider availability and realistic launch sequence. After closing, track the remaining tasks and compare actual spending with the approved plan. Keep the source documents and regular reports organized so later decisions rely on evidence from the property.
